review: i just moved to the area and have a new physician.  i saw him yesterday after having passed out in a store and getting an ambulance to st margaret's er. i was there 7 hours. they took an ekg and gave me one bag of fluids.  doc was shocked that they did not take at least a ct scan since i am post-stroke and this was my 3rd episode of syncope.  doc said avoid them if possible, but ok for imaging. he said he would never admit me there for anything overnight, especially surgery.

i was sent to the emergency room by my doctor. i had a very bad migraine and a blood pressure of 190/120. doc was concerned about a possible stroke and wanted my blood pressure to be brought down. i arrived at the emergency room at 1:30 pm. they immediately took my blood pressure which was 190/124. they immediately gave me an ekg, urine test, head ct scan and blood test. at 2:15, they then sent me back to the emergency room waiting area where i remained until 8 pm when i gave up and went to a real hospital. if i wanted to wait for freaking hours to see if i would have a stroke i would've done that at home in comfort where there's food. i was given no medication to bring the pressure down i was just told "we're busy, the wait is longer than usual." yeah, i believe the long wait is usual and so is their incompetence. if you are not good at the abcs of heathcare then you shouldn't be in operation. thank god for the university of chicago, a real hospital. fransiscan health hospital is a piece of shit.

someone close to my heart was admitted here into the psychiatric ward. however, i would not recommend that your loved one ends up here. it is extremely hard to contact the patient as you are told incorrect phone hours and are given the run around. if you are lucky enough to reach them, they can't identify the patient you are looking for. in my opinion, that is horrible being that it is a ward and the nurses should be aware of who is on their unit. after repeating the patients name several times, the man who answered the phone, hung up on me. i kept calling, but did not have any success. this man kept hanging up on me. i was extremely frustrated with how i was being treated so i put in a call to the nurses station. a nurse picked up and was able to identify who my loved one was, but told me "____ is sleeping". this seems to be their go-to when they don't feel like getting the patient. 
secondly, according to the patient, the nurses assumed he left the building and "couldn't" find him, however he was in his bed the whole time. this seems extremely unprofessional to me. also, apparently the food is not great. this person described this facility as jail, granted it's not supposed to be an all-inclusive resort, but they should have their ish together. 

overall, our family is not impressed with this facility and would not recommend it to anyone!

ok, full disclosure:  my long-term partner/husband is a doctor attached to this hospital (he's the hot plastic surgeon, hehe), along with a couple of others.  that said, this is a terrific hospital, in my independent opinion the best in the miami area, but it certainly has room for improvement.

it's located in weston, which although in the next county over, can be reached faster than some hospitals in miami itself (courtesy of a straight shot up i-75).   it's not a trauma center, so basically you have  to be conscious to ask the ambulance to take you here if an emergency.  weston's pretty posh, so not many stab or gunshot wounds out there.

i never pull the "my other half works here" card unless someone's really a tool, but they're almost invariably professional and highly competent from the front desk to the surgeon.  it's wholly owned and operated by the famous original cleveland clinic in ohio (splits the honors with mayo clinic and a few others in america for best hospital in the us).   they've just acquired a few regional hospitals in palm beach and martin counties, rebranding them cleveland clinic [insert city name here].

my one main gripe is the hospital so clearly targets the affluent, and neglects services for everyone else.  to their credit they don't cut any corners the way you might find in a giant teaching hospital in a rougher neighborhood.  that said, they're almost obnoxious about not marketing services in dade county, where half the population of southeast florida lives.  on the surface they claim it's because there is too much big-time competition in miami proper, but it seems more like they want to be sure they handle well-off well-insured suburbanites as patients.  it would make me give them 5 stars if they offered pro bono services for the folks who could really use it.

summary of my visit (full story below): a severe episode of food poison that did not require anything beyond water and some meds through iv, made me believe strongly that if this facility cannot properly handle even a case like mine, how could they handle properly (and humanely) a more complex case like many that they have in a regular day? if you read it and have a loved one that needs to go to an er in nyc, please make sure you consider other options in the city.

full story: i had an intense case of food poison and several violent episodes of vomit early on the evening of january 5th of 2020. around 8pm, i had no strength to continue throwing up and my partner brought me to the er at this hospital. 
after getting there and on the way to get my vitals (before being admitted to the er itself) my episodes of vomit were so violent and continuous that they had trouble even to have me seated straight to measure my blood pressure. at this moment, i basically dragged myself to the outside bathroom of the er so i could literally be on the ground with my face on the toilet, and avoid passing out.
when i was in this restroom, with the doors opened, one staff member came with a wheelchair because they realized i needed to go to the er immediately and "skip" the initial screening process. when they arrived there and saw me in the ground, with no strength and still vomiting, they simply said: "get yourself together". yes, i was in a miserable situation and these were the "greetings" i got on my way to the er. at this moment, my partner got extremely angry at them and he ended up being the one that helped me to get into the wheelchair.

when they got me in my slot in the er, we noticed that the place was not properly sanitary, let's say. the floors were not clean and the general appearance of the er was far from ideal. moreover, they were improvising new beds in the er by basically putting people in the halls of the facility.
from my arrival at the er bed until i finally had the iv, at least 2 hours had passed. i was vomiting in this whole period and lost track of how many times this happened. there was nothing left there, only the reflex of throwing up and at this point. i got so dehydrated at this point that (believe me) i could not even swallow anymore because my tongue and throat were too dry to allow this action to happen.
during this period, my partner asked doctors, nurses and whoever he could find in the er to initiate the iv so i could get some hydration and stop my episodes of vomiting. most of them were not happy with his several attempts to get someone to help me. the only doctor that was slightly more responsive (i think she was a supervisor in the er) said she would make sure to talk to doctors to initiate the treatment, but that was ineffective and did not happen until at least one hour after it.

long story short, two hours in the iv treatment were enough to improve my case by a lot, and therefore, my case was not complex enough to require more resources of the hospital. can you imagine what would potentially be the outcome if my case was something more complex, like pneumonia or a heart attack?

my question for the staff of this hospital is: given how many bad reviews you received through yelp beyond mine (not even considering the ones they might get outside here), would you bring a loved one to this er or would you be sensible enough to search for another hospital?
for those who are reading this, think twice before choosing this facility.

i came back to the er here recently in what was one of the worst decisions i could have made. i should have known better after my last visit.

what i experienced in icu here still gives me nightmares.

i waited over 8 hours after being triaged, with obvious symptoms of advanced pneumonia, including coughing up blood, shortness of breath and rapid breathing, severe and extreme confusion--all without anyone paying attention.

eventually, i started losing consciousness and apparently had gone into sepsis after waiting to be treated for so long.

the only reason i probably survived was that a hospital administrator (i believe her first name was sandra) happened to be nearby and intervened. she was horrified upon finding out how long i'd been waiting, and paged her medical director to see me. he showed up, then walked out when i had to go to the bathroom while talking to him. i forgot his name, but she fired him that same night after he refused to come back, and replaced him with dr. mathew.

upon my admission, a team separate from icu was assembled and confirmed a primary diagnosis of acute multi-focal pneumonia. despite this, a full course of antibiotics wasn't started until long after i'd been transferred out of icu. i was stabilized and given oxygen--for nearly 4 days--while still coughing up blood! dr. mathew was now supervising both critical care and icu, so there was no one watching over things most of the time.

now, i know how unbelievable it may sound, but my treatment was abruptly cut off and i was suddenly transferred to out of icu as a result of my bed in icu literally being sold to someone else.

this patient somehow walked into icu with his family and a lawyer, threatening to sue for previously poor treatment; they also offered an alternative: a huge sum of money just to get proper treatment. i overheard the panicked conversation, since my room was closest to the icu entrance, and all rooms there are kept open.

i was rushed out of icu under these truly bizarre circumstances.

this late-night, hushed maneuver must have resulted from a decision being approved at some high level by hospital administration. whether the motivation was money or fear of legal repercussions, putting patient care last is not only antithetical to the hippocratic oath, it's downright shameful, and the move was very likely illegal under state regulations.

i was so shocked by what i'd heard i initially said nothing when the nurse manager walked in and started to clear my room for that patient. she was clearly ashamed while disconnecting my iv line and oxygen (with my spo2 still dipping under 40%), then covering me up with a full bed-sheet.

i finally said, "i guess my my room is being given to someone else." she responded, "i guess you know everything." i was then told "you always have friends here," before being quickly wheeled out.

as deathly scary as that was, things only got worse.

once out of icu and out of sight of the new patient, i was handed only a small plastic bag of oxygen to breathe from. arriving in a medicine wing, the nurses alarmingly asked why there was no equipment to provide proper flow of oxygen.

as i found out eventually, i was transferred to a wing for palliative care; someone in icu must have been aware of this, since a portable oxygen machine was left anonymously in a plastic bag outside my room.

the wing i was transferred to was essentially a death ward. my vitals were checked only a handful of times in several days. the nurses' only job seemed waking me every hour, on the hour, to make sure i wasn't dead--there was no monitoring! i managed to negotiate a transfer to the main floor, 9, where actual medicine was practiced.

days later, when the cdc came back with results on the culture icu sent them, confirming a particularly bad strain of pneumonia, a full course of augmentin--a common antibiotic--was finally started.

to summarize, i nearly died in the er for lack of proper attention and treatment; was stabilized then received practically no treatment other than oxygen in icu for several days; had my bed there sold to someone else; was transferred to a palliative care wing--a death ward--before negotiating my way out; then was kept on medical hold, with my life upside down in the outside world, for 11 days--when i could have finished treatment at home.

review:
it makes me sad to have to give this hospital 3 stars.   the facilities and staff are terrific.    i have had 2 surgeries and 1 steroid injection at this facility.    some of my favorite dr's operate out of this facility.

unfortunately, i am extremely dissatisfied with their billing practices, especially after my last visit (steroid injection).

on all 3 occasions i have prepaid my hospital bills up front for the expected procedures.   in every case additional charges were added to the bill after insurance was billed.   these charges ranged from about 33-50% of the prepaid bill estimate.    

the final straw was the last visit for a steroid injection.   i probably spent an hour or less total in the prep room + surgery + recovery (only twilight sedation).   the final bill was over $4k just for the hospital portion before the insurance discount.   the bills for the surgeon and anesthesiologist portions were more than reasonable and are paid separately.   it's just the hospital charges that are way out of line.

the total cost of this procedure ended up being more than 5x the cost of my previous steroid injection done at another facility (same services).  

to me, the billing procedures at baylor employ some bait and switch practices.   the prepaid bill is based on an "estimate".   then, they expect the patient to cover additional expenses afterwards.    the insurance coverage is well spelled out beforehand.  so, there should not be any unexpected surprises for them after the fact.   my insurance company is probably the largest.    i am convinced that baylor knows ahead of time exactly what will be covered.

had i known that my out of pocket would have been a total of $2,350 (with insurance) ahead of time, i would have never scheduled this procedure at this location.    this is where i feel there is some bait and switch tactics going on, as the same thing has happened all 3 times that i have had procedures done here.    i personally believe they may be doing this to avoid "sticker shock" before the procedures.

my wife and i have had several medical procedures done at different hospitals over the last 2 years.    this is the only hospital that always seem to come up with phantom billing amounts after the fact.  

as i said, it makes me sad to write this, because there are some terrific doctors operating out of this facility.   and, the facility and staff are top notch.

if you can get baylor to agree to a fixed amount up front for your procedures, then i highly recommend this location.   if not, be prepared for some very large charges to be added to your bill later on.

we recently brought an immediate family member here for treatment of an acute reaction to a chemotherapy drug.  she spent 3 nights in critical care (icu), followed by 3 nights in the oncology unit.  the quality of care and attention she received was exceptional.  the nurses and physicians who managed her care were highly skilled and compassionate.  this facility is up-to-date and immaculately clean.

but since my forte is restaurant reviews, naturally i'm going to comment on the hospital's food service.  upgraded since our previous visit years ago, it's ably managed by sodexo, the france-headquartered institutional food service goliath (indeed, the french do know a thing or two about food prep).  inpatients receive a menu which includes rotating daily specials.  it's like room service at a fine hotel; you pick up the phone and order.  i'm told visitors can also order food.  food arrives within 30 minutes.  michelin stars my foot, but everything looked and smelled quite appetizing.

the oasis cafeteria on the first floor of the main building is open to hospital staff and visitors.  the missus and i dined here on two consecutive evenings.  their well-stocked salad bar is superior to those at many restaurants and groceries.  a special callout to the incredibly good 5-bean soup.  entrée choices were limited to just one or two main dishes, but the grill offers a variety of freshly-prepared hot sandwiches and there is also pizza.  i had a rather good grilled chicken sandwich one night and a decent quesadilla the next.  prices are very reasonable.

my pet peeve (with so many hospital cafeterias) is their short hours.  they close ridiculously early.  we are late eaters, and the chow line here gets locked down precisely at 6:30.  arrive at 6:31 and you're out of luck.  the only other meal option, a single vending machine dubbed "farmer's fridge," was completely empty during our visit.  thank goodness, a portillo's is located close by.

review:
my experience began by being transported to the emergency room for a fractured leg (both tibia and fibula) and two fractured ankles after suffering a fall.  immediately upon arrival, i was transferred to a gurney and awaited evaluation.  moments after i arrived another patient arrived via ambulance who was critically ill and required immediate staff attention (which i completely understood).  i had two injured legs but the other person certainly needed more care than i did. 

i'm lying on a gurney with two injured legs.  i realized my left leg was fractured to the point where it would require surgery (as the knee was pointing forward and the lower leg was completely turned to the left and sideways).  i hoped my right ankle just had a bad sprain (based on the significant amount of swelling) but i later learned it was fractured also.  

i realized i would need to walk on crutches in the near future so in order to spare my right ankle, i wanted to apply ice in an effort to prevent further swelling.  i asked my boyfriend to request a bag of ice from housekeeping.  he got a bag of ice and he applied it to my right ankle.  i then patiently waited for the staff to evaluate me.  the doctor arrived, evaluated me (she was very thorough and skillful).  she then ordered xrays....

i was transported via gurney for xrays of both legs.  a large xray tech picked up one leg at a time and placed it on a xray plate for imaging.  he picked up my left leg first and accidentally dropped it on the plate.  he then stated "maybe it's just a bad sprain".  upon witnessing the xray tech drop my leg, my boyfriend turned pale and had to sit down before he fainted.  at this point i was in so much pain i was practically numb.

i'll fast forward to surgery....
prior to being transported to the or for surgery and casting on both legs, i was supposed to receive a liquid oral medication that comes in a syringe.  the reason it came in a large syringe was because it was a syrup like pediatric medication that is normally given to a child orally.  the nurse arrives at my bedside saying she had the medication for me.  i was awaiting to take the medication by mouth when i suddenly noticed she injected it into my iv.  within seconds i experienced severe chest discomfort and thought i was having a heart attack.  i quickly realized what she had done and told her it was an oral med and not iv.  she replied "oh it can be given either way" (which is absolutely not true).  normally, i would have contacted the nursing supervisor immediately but as it was, i needed to be transported to the or for surgery.  what a nightmare.......

this is all a true story and it still boggles my mind that so many incompetent people can work in the same hospital.  the doctors were fantastic, the physical therapists were good, some of the nurses were great but some of the nurses (and xray tech) should not be practicing.

i was sent here from urgent care, who did a chest x-ray & an ekg.  they wanted me to get a d-dimer test (blood test) from an er, so i went here.  i explained this at the front desk & handed them the results of the ekg from urgent care.  i don't even think they looked at it.  they said they were going to do another x-ray & ekg based off my symptoms.  my naive 19 year old self had no idea how insurance works with emergency rooms & i had no clue that this would cost way more than some tiny copay.  they absolutely just wanted my money; there was no reason so redo these tests that i had just gotten done before coming here.

urgent care sent me here because my ekg results, along with my shortness of breath & chest tightness/pain, could have meant a blood clot.  it's a good thing i didn't have one, since i had to wait 5 hours to get the blood test.  took another hour for the results.  i understand that it's an er & things get busy, but come on- if it's suspected you might have a life-threatening issue, you really can't be waiting this long. 

not only will this hospital scam you after making you wait forever, but the care is just bad.  they did the x-ray & ekg shortly after i got there, but had me sit in the waiting room for about 4 hours after that.  then, they brought me back & had me sit in a chair in the hallway- didn't even get a room.  the nurse said he "needed to go check something with security" but he would "be right back".  i ended up sitting there for half an hour.  doc finally came & said they were going to do a d-dimer test.  i asked where i could get some water because i was insanely dehydrated, & he said he would bring me some.  then he was called away for an emergency.  so, from my chair, i asked the lady at the front desk the same question.  she said only the doctor can give me water because it might interfere with any tests they perform.  i explained that i was just doing a d-dimer & that the doc said he would bring me some but had to leave.  she seemed not to believe me and simply ignored me (this lady was also incredibly rude & unhelpful regarding my paperwork).  i was so dehydrated & felt awful.  i somehow fell asleep for a while until they finally came to do the test a while later. 

in short, this place just wants your money & doesn't care about its patients at all.  go to another er unless you have 5-6 hours to wait for rude & uncaring staff.

ok so i'm a nurse and always give the benefit of a doubt when someone writes a bad review of  a hospital. well here's another one. 
i took my friend into the er monday morning to igor before shift change. i wheeled her in and we approached the counter, no line. we stood there for five minutes while the intake person said absolutely nothing to us. as a seasoned healthcare worker i quickly surmised she was checking in the daughters of one of their employees. there is, however, always time to say "i'll be right with you, i'm checking these kids in". say something! well after a good five minutes standing next to my friend with her head hanging low the receptionist looked up and said "which one of you are checking in?" really? great. you can't even tell who's sick...so she doesn't ask what's wrong or what brings you in, just asks for id. 

triage went by quickly and then my friend was moved to a small room with a recliner. i joined her after i moved my car. bright glaring lights were on, no one to be found, she wasn't even introduced to her call light which was tightly wound around a bracket on the wall...nursing 101, a huge no no. 30 mins later a doctor comes in and assess the situation, going to get iv fluids, an ekg and anti nausea meds. ok thanks. 30 mins later the door opens, "we are going to draw blood". i'm sitting in the wheelchair. the attendant asks if i need the wheelchair, i assumed they were coming in to draw the blood since she announced that, and that only. i said "well if you take it i won't t have anywhere too sit". she looks at my friend and says "do you need it?" she responded "i'm good here in the recliner". attendant "well do you wanna walk?" ummm where? ohhhh are we going somewhere? yes to the treatment room. ohhhhhh well you didn't say that. ok so off to the treatment room.

she gets wheeled to a little waiting area outside another room and told "it will be just a second". we wait, and wait and wait.  i ask the nurses in the née they room if my friend could lie down, "it will be just a second, just a second". 30 mins later she i is invited back to another recliner. the nurse is just new off of maternity leave.  i got that from another employee who gleefully tells us after saying hello to her. i just need to know what our plans are thanks. these people have no customer service skills at all. 

they start the iv, give her anti nausea meds and something to relax her then tell us, "if it gets busy we may need to put you back out in this waiting area" whuuut?! yes, turns out my newly drugged friend may have to sit up in a chair, straight up, in a waiting area if they need her recliner. i said "are you serious? she's been vomiting all night and is weak and now medicated" the nurse replied "yes". i said "that's unacceptable" she replied "well that's what we have here" or something to that affect. i was ready to defend my friend's recliner at all costs...

two hours later, after the fluid is done we wait for someone to tell us the next move. i'm trying not to be that nurse so i just wait. an hour later i finally ask what happens next "well the doctor notified me he's in an emergency so it will be awhile". three hours later we leave....unnoticed.

this review is specifically for the emergency room.  i have actually had relatively positive experiences in other departments, which makes it all the more upsetting how bad the er was.

i had hit my head and had a cut that was bleeding.  it was in my hair so i couldn't really see it, but i didn't think it was too bad.  i hadn't lost consciousness or had any vision issues and the blood stopped after just a couple of minutes, but i knew i needed to be sewn up.  i spoke with the urgent care in the area, but they said i should probably head to an er.  "good" sam, here i come.

i got to the hospital and checked in to a basically empty er.  i told them what had happened, and since i knew i hadn't reached my deductible, i immediately asked how much it would cost.  well, of course, no one knows what the final charge will be, but they couldn't even give me a hint of the cost.  then i had to essentially sign away my life by saying that i would pay anything my insurance fails to cover.  i looked up the average cost of something that i had been through, and it was around $700.  here we go.

i fought the charges as much as i could for as long as i could, but of course i lost.  these people are all a bunch of money hungry jerks, taking advantage of people when they are in need.  it's pathetic.  i should have just gone to the urgent care and gotten faster and better service for $150.

the reasons why i have rated riverside as a three star is for two reasons. 

1. when having my gallbladder surgery, i had to have surgery twice. everyone knows that undergoing anesthesia is not safe nor cheap, but i had do it twice. the first time was to remove my gallbladder and gallstones. when i awoke, i was advised that some gallstones had been missed and that i would have to undergo surgery again the next day to remove the remaining stones. let's not go into detail about that nor discuss my anesthesiology bill. 

2. the billing department for the hospital has some of the rudest and most non-empathetic individuals i have ever encountered! they would not work with me in regards to my $12,000 bill i had accrued in less than six weeks. i had a $4,000 deductible through my insurance so they charged me $4,000 for me when giving birth (in december), $4,000 for my daughter when she was born, and then $4,000 for my gallbladder surgery (in january). the only payment plan they offered to work with me on was a 12 month - $1,000 month plan. this also did not include the numerous separate bills that i received from anesthesiology and some other medical offices. they immediately sent me to collections after three months since i could not afford their $1,000 per month payment plan - especially with being on maternity leave for eight weeks. 

now that i am on a better insurance plan (far less deductible), i may consider using riverside again if for some reason any medical emergency arise. my tip to others is that you better make sure you're on a pretty good insurance plan before visiting riverside as their billing department is not one that you want to work with! koop

my son recently had major surgery at chla. not only were the doctors and nurses attentive and helpful, but they did a great job of helping him recover quickly. 

they gave him a stuffed toy during his pre-op, gave us blankets the day of the operation while we waited, and the nurses always tried to make him and us comfortable.

when he was in icu, the nurses listened to us when we thought he was in pain and did whatever they could. the doctors and nurses communicated everything they were doing to us so we were aware and asked us if we were ok with things.

there is a lot of chaos at this hospital- if you are there you hear the helicopter coming frequently. when we were there some emergencies happened in other rooms as we heard the alarms. for all the staff is dealing with, they try to make everything as calm and helpful as possible. even when we would mention the chaos, they responded in a way that wasn't alarming. they do a great job of not scaring families but at the same time keeping you in the loop with your child. in icu they even let the parents attend the morning meeting where the doctors and nurses are discussing your child's care plan.

we were discharged pretty quickly which was the only thing that felt rushed, but i'm pretty sure they needed the room and my son was recovering well enough to go home. 

we had to go to the emergency room recently because of a possible issue from surgery. turns out it wasn't anything, but we needed to check. that experience was also good. yes, emergency rooms are crowded, with long wait times, and lots of sick people, like many people have mentioned in the reviews. that's typical of an er. as with any other emergency room, priority is given to the more urgent cases. we got in pretty quickly considering, and we were out within a few hours. 

the food at the cafe is good considering it's hospital food. that's a separate review i'll review specifically for the hbo cafe, but the only thing i'll mention here other than good food is be wary of dinner- it's the same food from lunch, so if you come later in the evening, they may not have much selection.

the only other thing i could say that's not positive is there was not clarity about giving blood before surgery. we were under the impression it was part of the pre op process. however, we found out that day that we really should have done it days before if we wanted it to be ready for our son for his surgery. chla has a large blood bank so it is not an issue, but good to know if you want to give blood for your child. they said many parents come back after to give blood for another child who may need it.

positive note, max parking per day is $10, and there is a parking pass for a week for $40. these are great rates for la and i'm happy they've done this. note on the parking though, the garage gets very full and sometimes it takes a while to get out. prepare accordingly for arrival and leaving. 

another positive, they have a full on farmers market on wednesday's, which is very nice if you're there with your child.

overall, chla is a great place considering how sad it is to see so many kids who are there. it's an eye opening place that has staff that do what they can to make it more positive, help kids heal, and bring smiles. 

i'm not sure why there are so many negative reviews. it seems most of them are about the emergency department and people who do not understand how that process goes, so please don't let those deter you from going here- whether to see a doctor, have a surgery, or to the er. it's a great place that takes care of kids!

miami healthcare exec philip esformes found guilty of paying kickbacks and bribes
by jay weaver and david ovalle
april 05, 2019 10:15 am 
philip esformes is a miami beach healthcare executive at the center of a massive medicare fraud case.
philip esformes is a miami beach healthcare executive at the center of a massive medicare fraud case. rob latour rob latour/invision/ap
philip esformes, an obsessive businessman who built an empire of healthcare facilities in miami-dade, was found guilty friday of 20 charges, including paying bribes and kickbacks, in a scheme to generate streams of medicare patients for his businesses.

the wealthy miami beach executive managed his chain of skilled-nursing and assisted-living facilities with an iron hand, with prosecutors arguing he had billed $1 billion to the federal health insurance program for questionable services that patients largely didn't need or even receive.

esformes faced 26 charges overall. the 12-person federal jury, after three full days of deliberation, came back with guilty verdicts on most of them in what was touted as the biggest medicare fraud case in the country -- in the reputed capital of such criminal activity, miami. jurors, however, did not reach a verdict on the main count -- that esformes had conspired to defraud the taxpayer-funded medicare progra

 

esformes, 50, went to trial alone in february because two key conspirators -- a physician's assistant and a former larkin hospital administrator who recycled patients for cash -- had pleaded guilty. several other healthcare associates charged with medicare fraud in related cases had also pleaded guilty and cooperated with federal prosecutors, including some who testified against him.




 1:32feds break up largest medicare scam in u.s. history

the u.s. attorney's office held a press conference in miami on july 22, 2016, announcing the filing of charges in connection with a $1 billion medicare care fraud scheme. by logan riely
esformes, who was arrested in july 2016 and has been held without bond at the federal detention center, could spend the rest of his life in prison, even without a healthcare fraud conspiracy conviction. he faces a forfeiture hearing before the jury on monday. no sentencing date has been set before u.s. district judge robert scola.

one of esformes' defense attorneys, roy black, focused on the fact that the jury was hung on the indictment's main conspiracy count of defrauding the medicare program.

"for three years, they [prosecutors] have touted this case as a $1 billion healthcare fraud and they failed to prove it," black said.

"the jury was unable to reach a verdict on that and several other counts; however, they did obviously find him guilty of a number [of other counts]," black added. "it's certainly a mixed bag."

the deadlocked verdict on the main conspiracy count was puzzling to some legal observers because jurors found esformes guilty of bribery and paying and receiving kickbacks to generate medicare patients for his facilities as well as those of other healthcare operators. it is possible that some of the jurors believed esformes' facilities provided healthcare services to patients and therefore did not technically fleece the federal program.

despite the mixed results, especially on the hung healthcare fraud count, the justice department declared total victory.

"philip esformes orchestrated one of the largest healthcare fraud schemes in u.s. history, defrauding medicare and medicaid to the tune of over a billion dollars," said assistant attorney general brian a. benczkowski of the justice department's criminal division. "i commend our dedicated prosecutors and law enforcement partners for their professionalism and unyielding pursuit of justice on behalf of american taxpayers and vulnerable beneficiaries who, as a result of esformes' crimes, were denied the level of care that they needed and deserved."

at trial, convicted healthcare operators, the former hospital administrator and an ex-ivy league basketball coach testified that esformes paid them and various doctors hundreds of thousands of dollars in bribes to buy and sell patients as well as to get his son into the university of pennsylvania. esformes himself made $38 million from medicare and medicaid payments between 2010 and 2016.

"ladies and gentlemen, the amount of cash was staggering," justice department lawyer allan medina said in a packed miami federal courtroom during closing arguments last week. "when you commit fraud of this magnitude, it's a win-win for all the partners in crime. philip esformes has a commodity, the patients. philip esformes has the doctors to do what he wants them to do."

unfortunately, going to the er at ojai valley community hospital (ovch) in recent years has become a little like playing a game of russian roulette with a couple rounds in the cylinder.  
   between 5 active, athletic kids and my own injuries, we've been there dozens of times over nearly 20 years. and in most cases it i'd describe our experiences as pretty good - as far as a trip to the emergency room goes. 
   however in the past few years that's changed, and seems to be getting progressively worse.  and our recent january 2020 er visit didn't help improve my opinion. 
   why the decline?  one big reason is that  ovch has been "contracting out"  it's emergency room services to what i'd describe as out of town medical "mercenaries" who come in and gouge the hospital and the patient.  they have no connection to the community, no affiliation with the hospital, and are essentially accountable to no one. they won't even tell you that your medical insurance is no good with them. it's insane. 
   even if ovch is part of your insurance plan and is recommended by your insurance carrier as your emergency care facility......even if you make your er co-payent to ovch when you check in at the emergency room desk..... these unethical parasite physicians will bill you separately for their er care because (as "contract physicians") they simply don't have to accept your medical insurance.  
problem is - you'll never know that until you subsequently receive their bill in the mail!  
   that's a sign to me that ovch has recently become hard-up for doctors / nurses and is failing the community with it's overall lack of oversight.  **the ovch foundation board needs to take action.   
   in fairness i'd say that as long as the er physician on duty happens to be one of the good local docs like doug nelson or gordon clawson (and a few others)  you're in competent care.  and if you're able to confirm beforehand (before any care is rendered) exactly who your er doc is going to be and that he/she fully accepts your insurance as full payment (get it in writing), you're probably ok from at least a billing perspective.
   if not i'd head immediately to cottage hospital in santa barbara or to saint john's hospital in oxnard where you'll get far more comprehensive (and much faster) care.  it'll be worth the drive and peace of mind.

review:
the good: the nurses, doctors and support staff largely make a herculean effort to care for those who find themselves at this ancient medical facility. hugely grateful to them for saving my life. 

the bad: this was, without question, the dirtiest, most poorly designed, badly run hospital, with the most limited facilities, i have ever witnessed. 

summary: 9 hours in the shockingly dirty er which seems to operate much as one would anticipate in a third world country. 2-1/2 days in an equally filthy er room, while going through a battery of tests. several hours in surgery, which was very professional on all accounts. 2-1/2 days on the first floor ward, which was (again) shockingly dirty and poorly outfitted.

besides the excellent staff, this hospital is terrifyingly bad. apparently, nobody ever takes a shower here, as when one can find a shower, it appears to have last been cleaned in 1998. everything about this place (besides most of the staff) smacks of stunning disregard for the patient's comfort and wellbeing. i never saw anybody cleaning, beyond taking out the trash. there was visible dirt everywhere, save for the surgery and scanning areas. the blankets are as thin as paper and threadbare. ditto for the towels, if you can get your hands on one. 

the business office visited me twice, while i was doubled over in pain, waving documents and asking for money on the spot, in spite of my $1160 monthly premium being fully paid up -- and offering no specific details about what i was being charged for. apparently, my hospital co-pay is $1400, which they wanted on the spot, with zero itemisation. 

though i am grateful to the nurses and doctors who saved my life, i hope to never return to this hospital again.

the doctors and nurses are very caring, very professional, super informative and want you to be comfortable and to heal.  they ran blood work 3 times, an ecg and then had ecg monitoring, a ct scan, and a chest x-ray, all because i may have had a heart attack, stroke or mini-stroke.

hca must pay $162 million for charity care problems

healthcare giant hca, based in nashville, tn, must pay a kansas city, mo, charitable foundation $162 million and undergo extensive auditing after a judge found that the for-profit hospital operator broke key agreements regarding charity care and capital expenditures in its billion-dollar purchase of hospitals from health midwest in 2002.

judge john torrence, jd, of the circuit court of jackson county, mo, ruled that hca, the nation's largest investor-owned hospital company, did not spend as much money improving health midwest's existing facilities as it said it would. the judge also ruled that hca did not abide by an agreement to provide at least as much charity care to the community as the health midwest's not-for-profit hospitals had provided before the sale. that amount was said to be $65 million annually.

the health care foundation of greater kansas city (hcf) had sued hca in october 2009 to ensure that it had complied with its more than $950 million obligation to charity care in the kansas city area. the purpose of the lawsuit was to determine if hca had complied with its obligations to make $450 million in capital improvements to existing health midwest facilities and provide over $500 million in charity care. hcf chairman karen cox, rn, supported the ruling, saying "as a voice for the uninsured and underserved, the hcf board of directors felt it had the fiduciary responsibility to make sure that this population had been afforded the services promised to them through the sale of health midwest."

hca issued a statement saying it would appeal the decision. "rather than simply put money into the repair of old facilities, we built two new hospitals, spending hundreds of millions of dollars to ensure this community has high quality care," the company said in a written statement. "we believe we have complied with our agreement, exceeded our promises, and we continue to spend millions for the benefit of a community we love."

health midwest had operated 11 not-for-profit hospitals in missouri and kansas before the sale.

excellent hospital for giving birth in the bay area

we had two of our babies born here (3 years apart) at the sequoia "dignity health" hospital. both times we had a very pleasant experience. we found that virtually all the nurses were very well trained and highly experienced. we found that they were very caring for the health of the mother and the baby. i know a couple of our friends also gave birth in this hospital and were very happy. generally, it is not super crowded like some other hospitals and feels very clean and premium hospital. 

nurses:
i believe that each nurse are assigned to manage 2 patients during their shift. and there are two shifts (7am-7pm and 7pm-7am). so expect two main nurse assigned to you each day you are there. there are also other nurses who do some specific things, who keep coming in-and-out during the stay. they also have monitors in their lobby areas where they constantly monitor all the patients. one of the things that really impressed me is their team work. all the nurses were genuinely helping each other even when they were not assigned directly to the patient. 

emergency situations:
giving birth is a very complex thing and is really a miracle! at any given point in time, there could be an emergency! each room is equipped with emergency buttons that the mothers can push and it literally creates an ambulance like noise in the nurses' break rooms and control rooms with red-lights blinking above the patient's door and alerts every nurse about it. and both times we were there, some patients pressed their emergency buttons in the middle of the night for different reasons and i saw all these nurses literally running and rushing to that room to help that patient! it was really amazing to see them caring so much! this is the main reason i gave 5-stars! 

they also have a couple of in-house obgyn doctor (at least 1, 24x7) and couple of in-house anesthesiologists to take care of things in addition to nurses.

birthing room:
each birthing room has a fancy birthing bed with a lot of special capabilities to help with birthing. the bed also has a bunch of buttons to articulate the bed, plus there is a tv that the mother (or spouse) can watch while waiting for the baby to arrive. next to the bed, they have a small bed for the spouse or relative to take some rest (if that's possible). 
each room also has an attached restroom with a toilet, sink and a shower.

hospital food:
hospital food, especially for vegetarians like us was pretty blonde and terrible :( we suspected it and so we actually cooked food at home and brought it to the hospital, so it was not much of an issue. i hope non-vegetarian foods are better, but i encourage you to do the same as we did :)

postpartum:
one thing i've heard is that during some months it does become quite busy and after the birth, they'll move the mom and baby from the main birth room to a different smaller room during the 48 hours recovery period. i know one of our friends were moved but we were not.

i believe the hospital also has other departments, and i don't know anything about them but if you are planning to have a baby, i highly recommend this center and am sure this is one of the best in the bay area. 

btw, after the birth, make sure to give the nurses cookies and chocolates to thank them!
